Stage 1 · Warm-up

Bored!

Boredom is not the absence of things to do. It is having things to do and wanting none of them.

Stage 4 · Other uses of -ing and to + verb

Where each form goes when there is no verb in front of it

Lesson 33 was about what follows a verb. This is everything else: subjects, prepositions, purposes, adjectives, and too and enough.

The single most useful rule here: after a preposition, always -ing. That covers with, about, of, at, after, before, instead of, without, and the to in look forward to and be used to, which is a preposition and not an infinitive.

4 · One idea, six frames.
Waiting is the worst part.  →  subject.
I am fed up with waiting.  →  after a preposition.
I came early to avoid the queue.  →  purpose.
There is nothing to do here.  →  after a noun.
It is impossible to concentrate.  →  it is + adjective.
Three hours is too long to sit still.  →  too + adjective.
1 · Read the explanation.
Where each form goes

The -ing form as a noun. It can be the subject (Doing the ironing is boring), the object (I hate queuing), or come after be (The worst part is waiting). English almost never uses an infinitive as a subject in speech: To do the ironing is boring is grammatical and sounds like a translation.

After a preposition, always -ing. fed up with waiting, tired of being told, instead of leaving, without asking, after finishing, before starting. Watch the phrases that end in to, where to is a preposition and not part of an infinitive: look forward to seeing you, be used to working late, object to being interrupted.

To + verb for purpose. I left early to catch the train answers why. In formal writing you will also see in order to and so as to, and their negatives in order not to, so as not to.

To + verb after nouns and adjectives. nothing to do, a reason to stay, the first person to arrive; desperate to leave, ready to go, hard to explain. Also after it is + adjective: It is difficult to concentrate.

Too and enough. too tired to argue, old enough to know better, enough work to keep me occupied. The negative always goes in front of the form: hard not to fall asleep, fed up with not having enough to do.

The commonest errors at this level
  • I am fed up with wait or fed up with to wait.
  • I look forward to see you — that to is a preposition.
  • To do the ironing is boring as an opening sentence in speech.
  • I came here for buy a ticket instead of to buy.
  • It is difficult concentrating when you mean It is difficult to concentrate.

Two things to watch

1 — Test whether to is a preposition. If you can put a noun after it (look forward to the weekend), it is a preposition, so the verb takes -ing.

2 — For does not introduce a purpose with a verb. I came here to buy a ticket, not for buy. For works with a noun: I came here for a ticket.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Deciding which form a gap needs

The sentence: I am fed up with ______ (wait) for the train.

Step 1 — look at the word immediately before the gap. It is with, a preposition. That settles it: waiting. No meaning question arises.

The second sentence: I left the house early ______ (catch) the earlier train.

Step 2 — ask what the gap is doing. It answers why did you leave early. That is a purpose, so the form is to catch.

The third sentence: ______ (wait) is the worst part of travelling.

Step 3 — find the subject. There is no subject before the verb, so the gap itself is the subject: Waiting.

In short: preposition before it → -ing. Answering why → to + verb. Standing where a noun would stand → -ing. After a noun or an adjective → to + verb.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Where -ing goes when no verb is in front of it

As a subject: Waiting is the worst part · Doing the ironing is boring. English does not open a sentence with to wait here. After be: The worst part is waiting. After any preposition: fed up with waiting · tired of being told what to do — and the rule holds with no exceptions.

The trap is the phrases where to is a preposition, not part of an infinitive: look forward to seeing you · be used to working late · object to paying. If you can put a noun after it (look forward to the weekend), it is a preposition, and the verb after it takes -ing. go + activity is also -ing: go swimming, go shopping.

Where the infinitive goes

Purpose — the answer to why?: I left early to catch the train. The formal version is in order to, and the negative purpose is in order not to wake anybody, never to not wake in careful writing. After a noun: nothing to do, a reason to stay, a way to leave. After an adjective: desperate to get off. After it is + adjective: It is hard to concentrate. After too / enough: too tired to argue · enough work to keep me occupied — note that too goes before the adjective and enough after it, but before a noun.

Negatives put not first, in both forms: hard not to fall asleep · fed up with not having enough work. And both forms have passives: tired of being told · desperate to be told something useful.

Errors to watch: To wait is the worst part in ordinary English → Waiting is · I look forward to see you → to seeing · I am used to work late → to working · too tired for arguing → too tired to argue · enough tired → tired enough.

1 · Read the model.
Model · an opinion piece in four paragraphs

Being bored is treated as a fault in the design of a day, something to be removed with a phone. I think we have confused two states that feel similar and do completely different things. Doing nothing in order to unwind is rest. Doing nothing because there is nothing worth doing is boredom, and boredom is where most of my ideas have come from.

The argument against me is strong and I want to state it properly. Most boredom is not chosen. Sitting through a dull lecture, listening to a boss who cannot get to the point, waiting three hours in an airport: nobody produces anything in those hours, and pretending they are secretly valuable is a way of excusing whoever designed them. Being trapped is the problem, not being unstimulated.

That is fair, and it leaves my case intact. The boredom worth protecting is the kind you can walk out of. Last winter I spent four evenings too tired to read and too awake to sleep, fed up with everything I owned, and it was in the fourth of them that I finally worked out why a project had been failing for a year. Nothing entertaining happened. My mind wandered, and it wandered somewhere useful.

So I would not remove boredom; I would separate it from being trapped. I have stopped reaching for my phone in queues, which is a small thing and the only one I have managed to keep.
